phonemes.desc: Short epsilon [e], the prepositional prefix ἐπί- opening the name.
Plain pi [p], unaspirated as in Greek spelling before another consonant.
Long eta [ɛː] with acute pitch — the stressed peak of the name.
Aspirated theta [tʰ], the same root that gives Promētheus his 'forethought'.
Long upsilon with acute, the agent-noun ending: 'the one who thinks'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'eh-pee-MAY-thay-oos' — stress falls on the long middle syllable; the final syllable is held and ends with an -oos sound.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ἐπιμηθεύς (Epimētheús), the brother of Promētheus in Hesiod (Theogony 510)

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Epimetheus, the form preserved in Roman mythography (Hyginus, Fabulae 142-143)

pronunciation.note: Epimētheus is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἐπιμηθεύς carries both stress (acute on the long ē and on the final ū) and length (ē, ūs), distinctive features the ASCII form flattens.

domains.title: The Afterthinker
domains.subtitle: Hindsight, Rash Acceptance, and the Release of Evils
domains.lead: Epimētheus is the twin brother of Promētheus, but where his brother thinks ahead, Epimētheus thinks behind. In Hesiod he is the one who accepts Pandora — the all-gifted woman — and with her the jar that releases sorrow, toil, and disease into the human world. His name is not a flaw in Greek; it is a role: the necessary complement to foresight, the moment after the choice when consequence becomes visible.

cards.name: The Jar of Evils
cards.desc: Hesiod says Epimētheus took the great storage-jar's lid and scattered evils among mortals; only Elpis, Hope, remained inside (Works and Days 90-105).

cards.name: Pandora
cards.desc: The 'all-gifted' woman fashioned by the gods and sent to Epimētheus as a punishment for Promētheus's theft of fire (Hesiod, Works and Days 60-82).

cards.name: Brother of Forethought
cards.desc: Promētheus warns him never to accept a gift from Zeus; Epimētheus forgets the warning and acts on impulse (Works and Days 83-89).

cards.name: Aftermath
cards.desc: His myth turns on the moment after: the recognition that some gifts are also judgments, and that hindsight arrives one heartbeat too late.

symbols.name: The storage-jar (pithos)
symbols.meaning: The household vessel from which every human ill escaped, and in which Hope alone remained — a kitchen jar, which is precisely Hesiod's bitter point

symbols.name: Pandora
symbols.meaning: The crafted gift he accepted, embodying both allure and consequence — a 'beautiful evil' sent by Zeus

symbols.name: Brother pair
symbols.meaning: Forethought and afterthought as two sides of mortal decision: Promētheus sees ahead, Epimētheus sees behind

symbols.name: The forgotten warning
symbols.meaning: The advice he received and could not keep — the emblem of every precaution remembered after the door has opened

symbols.name: Ember or fading flame
symbols.meaning: The aftermath of Promētheus's fire — the heat that remains when the moment of choice has passed

mythology.lead: Epimētheus appears most fully in Hesiod's didactic poems and Plato's Protagoras, where he is less a hero than a caution: the type of mortal who acts first and understands later. His small cluster of myths is the Greek anatomy of hindsight.

myths.title: The Brother Given the Job
myths.text: In Plato's Protagoras (320c-322d), the gods mold mortal creatures from earth and fire and assign Promētheus and Epimētheus the job of equipping each kind with its powers: Epimētheus persuades his brother to let him distribute, while Promētheus inspects. Epimētheus — true to his name — hands out strength, speed, claws, hides, wings, and hooves until every species is protected; then he looks at the naked human being, 'still unprovided with its portion,' and realizes the stock is spent. Promētheus must steal fire and the mechanical arts from Athena and Hephaestus to keep the bare, shoeless, unbedded creature alive. The myth defines the human being by an original clerical error: we are the species whose equipment ran out, and whose survival has depended ever since on borrowed fire and compensating craft.

myths.title: Take Nothing From Zeus
myths.text: After Zeus had Promētheus bound for the theft of fire, he devised a second punishment: the fashioned Pandora, sent to earth with a great storage-jar as her dowry. Hesiod's Works and Days (83-89) records the crucial detail — 'before this' Promētheus had warned his brother never to accept a gift from Olympian Zeus, but to send it back, 'so that no evil come to mortals.' Epimētheus heard the warning and forgot it in the moment it mattered: 'he took the evil, and only when he had it perceived the evil.' Apollodorus (Library 1.7.2) compresses the same scene. The myth is a miniature anatomy of hindsight: the warning exists, it is known, it is even repeated — and it is useless one heartbeat after the door opens. Every later retelling, from Apollodorus to the modern proverb about gifts from above, is a footnote to that single line of Hesiod's.

myths.title: All the Evils Fly Out
myths.text: Hesiod tells the rest with terrible economy (Works and Days 90-105). Epimētheus lifted the lid of the great jar — a pithos, not the later 'box' — and out flew the thousand sorrows that wander among mortals: toil, disease, old age, famine, every bane that had never before touched the human day, for before Pandora 'the tribes of men lived on earth free from ills... without the evil diseases that bring death.' Only Hope — Elpis — stayed inside, caught beneath the rim, because Pandora replaced the lid 'by the plans of aegis-bearing Zeus,' Hesiod adds, darkly, before the hope can console. The myth refuses to say whether hope remaining is mercy or the last cruelty: the one blessing left is also the one still sealed away, and Hesiod will not resolve it for us.

myths.title: The Price of Fire
myths.text: Hesiod's Theogony (570-616) tells the Pandora story from the gods' side and makes Epimētheus its hinge. Zeus orders Hephaestus to mix earth and water into 'a beautiful evil,' Athena to dress her, Aphrodite and Hermes to load her with longing and lies; then 'he sent her, a gift, to Epimētheus,' who 'took no heed of Promētheus' charge never to accept a gift from Zeus — and when the evil was his, he understood.' From her descend 'the race of women,' a 'great pain for mortal men' — the passage is Hesiod at his most bitter, and later Greeks themselves flinched from it. Read against the Works and Days, the two tellings bracket the human condition: afterthought inherits forethought's warning, forgets it, and that single lapse is why the jar stands open in every house.

lore.syncretism: Epimētheus has no Roman cult or foreign double; his afterlife is philosophical and literary. The Platonic Protagoras retells the distribution of qualities as a lesson in human lack and compensation, and later Platonists read the two brothers as faculties of the soul. Renaissance and Enlightenment writers used him as an emblem of impulsive judgment, and modern risk theory borrows his name for the habit of acting before consequences are understood — 'epimethean' thinking. His closest mythic kin is his own brother: Promētheus is the crime, Epimētheus is the regret, and the Greek tradition keeps them chained to each other as tightly as the Titan to his rock.
lore.culturalLegacy: Epimētheus survives in the language of hindsight. Every proverb about looking before leaping, every warning against opening Pandora's box, every discussion of unintended consequences rehearses his story. In cognitive science and economics, 'epimethean' thinking names the backward glance that reorganizes judgment after the fact — the post-mortem, the audit, the lesson learned. The jar he opened cannot be closed, but Hope remains inside it, and second thoughts, which are his true gift to mortals, are the beginning of conscience. The restoration Epimētheus keeps the Greek stress and length that mark him as the necessary twin of forethought.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Epimētheus is the god every human being meets in the small hours. He is the one who says, 'If only I had known,' the one who understands the warning only after the jar is open. His myth is not an invitation to despise him but to recognize him: we are all, at some moment, the afterthinker. The jar he opened cannot be closed, but Hope remains inside it — not as a remedy, but as the thing that makes the next opening possible.

To meditate on Epimētheus is to meditate on the irreversibility of choice. His name means afterthought, and afterthought is where wisdom is born, always too late for the mistake that fathered it. Yet without it there would be no learning, no regret, no change of mind. He is the patron of second thoughts, and second thoughts are the beginning of conscience.

lore.archaeology: Epimetheus is a purely textual figure: no sanctuary, cult image, or votive inscription names him. His witnesses are the manuscripts of Hesiod and Plato, the Attic ceramic tradition that depicts Pandora and the jar, and the long afterlife of the myth in Western literature and philosophy. His absence from the archaeological record is itself informative — the Greeks personified hindsight in words, not in cult.
